title: Fire
summary: Gather all your tinder, kindling and fuel first, then build and light the fire outdoors. Never leave it unattended. Fireplaces and wood stoves have their own topic.

list: Tinder: dry, fine material that a spark can light. Birch bark, dead dry grass, cattail or milkweed fluff, fine shavings of pine pitch wood, lint, cotton balls coated with petroleum jelly. Collect at least a cupped handful.
Kindling: dead, dry twigs in several sizes, from pencil-lead to thumb thickness, about 12 to 18 inches long. Collect a bundle as thick as a soda can of each size.
Fuel: dead wood at least as thick as your forearm. Dry dead branches snap when broken. Skip rotten wood lying on the ground: it smolders.

blocks.p: If you skip the tinder or kindling stage, the fire will likely fail.

steps: Pick a flat, dry spot out of the wind, away from overhanging branches and snow-loaded trees. Clear leaves, needles and anything else that burns from a 10-foot circle, and scrape at least the middle 3 feet down to bare soil.
On deep snow, build on a base of green logs laid in two layers, crosswise. Never use wet, porous or riverbed rocks: they can explode when heated.
Put the tinder in the centre and lean kindling around it like a teepee. Light it from the upwind side, then add kindling and fuel from small to large.
Once it’s going, a log cabin of fuel stacked in crosswise layers around it quickly makes a large bed of coals for cooking.

blocks.cap: On deep snow, build on green logs in two crosswise layers. Never use wet, porous or riverbed rocks: they can explode when heated.
Start with a teepee; build a log cabin around it once it catches.

list: In the cold, green logs up to about the thickness of a soda can break easily, so you can gather them by hand for the base. Make the base big enough to hold the whole fire, so the coals can’t melt a hole down through the snow (Army ATP 3-50.21).
In extreme cold, green wood dries out and becomes a usable fuel (Army ATP 3-50.21).
In extreme cold, lighter fuel can freeze and the lighter won’t work. Warm it with your body heat first (Army ATP 3-50.21).

sections.h: Fire lays for heat and cooking

blocks.p: The teepee lights fast and the log cabin makes coals for cooking (above). Other lays the Army uses:

list: Long fire, for heat and cooking: lay two logs, green if you can, at least 6 inches (15 cm) thick, side by side to hold the coals between them, and close enough that pots can rest on them. Put a 1-inch (2.5 cm) stick under both logs at each end so the coals get more air. More people can sit near the heat, and you can rake coals to one end to cook while the fire burns at the other (Army ATP 3-50.21).

Star fire, to save fuel: lay logs like the spokes of a wheel with their inner ends in the fire, and push each one in as its end burns. It lets you burn logs too big to break up. It must be tended all the time. Hardwood works best (Army ATP 3-50.21).

Pyramid, a long, slow fire: lay two small logs side by side on the ground and a solid layer of small logs across them. Add three or four more layers, each smaller than the last and crosswise to the one below. Light a small fire on top; it burns down through the layers (Army ATP 3-50.21). The Army says it needs no attention overnight. This app still says never leave a fire unattended, and asleep counts as unattended (see Put it out).

Cross-ditch, for a draft: scrape an X about 12 inches (30 cm) across and 3 inches (8 cm) deep. Put the tinder in the middle and a small pyramid of kindling over it. Air flows along the ditch under the tinder (Army ATP 3-50.21).

blocks.p: For heat and less smoke, burn dry, split hardwood such as oak, hickory or ash. Softwoods such as pine, spruce and fir burn faster and make more smoke unless you keep a large flame going, but are easier to split (Army ATP 3-50.21).

list: A reflector throws the fire’s heat where you want it and keeps the wind from carrying the heat away (Army ATP 3-50.21). Use it to send heat into the open side of a lean-to (below), not into an enclosed shelter.
Build it before you light the fire: that is much harder once the fire is hot (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Make it of green logs or dry, solid rock. Never use wet, porous or riverbed rocks: they can explode when heated (Army ATP 3-50.21).
With a lean-to, the fire goes in front of the open side and the reflector on the far side of the fire, so the heat comes back into the shelter (Shelter).

Reflector wall for a lean-to in cold weather: drive four stakes about 5 feet (1.5 m) long into the ground. Stack green logs between them in two rows, with a gap between the rows, and fill the gap with dirt. Tie the tops of the stakes together so the logs and dirt stay in place. The dirt makes the wall stronger and reflect more heat (Army ATP 3-50.21).

Ferro rod (metal match): hold the rod with its tip at the tinder. Hold the striker or a knife at a right angle to the rod and drive it down the rod with firm, even pressure so the sparks land in the tinder.

Battery and fine steel wool: stretch fine steel wool across both posts of the battery. It heats up and makes a glowing coal to light the tinder. Keep flames away from the battery: some batteries give off explosive hydrogen gas.
Bow drill: it works, but it takes a lot of effort and practice. Learn it before you need it.

blocks.cap: Ferro rod. Hold the rod with its tip at the tinder and drive the striker down the rod, at a right angle to it.

blocks.p: In wet weather, use standing or leaning dead wood (it sheds rain), the dead lower branches under conifers, and split wood to reach the dry inner wood. A teepee fire burns well even with wet wood.

list: Keep tinder and kindling off wet ground: build on a dry base, such as a flat piece of wood or dry, solid rock (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Dry damp tinder by carrying it between layers of your clothes, where your body heat reaches it (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Fuel doesn’t have to be completely dry once the fire is going well enough to dry it before it burns. The wetter the fuel, the more white smoke (Army ATP 3-50.21).
As a last resort, green wood will burn if it is finely split and mixed evenly with dry, dead wood (Army ATP 3-50.21).

Shield a lit match from the wind. Hold it head down at an angle so the flame climbs the stick, then hold it at the bottom edge of the tinder without pushing it in and smothering it (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Never burn wood with poison ivy or poison oak on it: the smoke can cause breathing problems (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Carry matches (waterproof if you can) or a lighter, and fire starters: things that catch fire quickly and keep a flame going (National Park Service).
Keep matches in a waterproof container with a striker. Matches with wax-coated tips are sold, or dip the heads in melted wax yourself (Army ATP 3-50.21).
A butane lighter stands up to wind better and burns hotter than a liquid-fuel lighter (Army ATP 3-50.21).
A ferro rod works wet or dry, hot or cold, and doesn’t go off with age. Quality varies, so try yours before you need it, and keep it from rusting (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Pack man-made tinder, such as cotton balls coated with petroleum jelly (see Gather everything first).
Learn the local fire rules before you go (National Park Service). New York’s are below.

blocks.p: These steps are for outdoor fires. A fire in a fireplace or wood stove has its own rules: put it out before you go to sleep, with no fire watch, and never pour water into the chimney. See Wood stoves and fireplaces.

Never leave a fire unattended. To put it out, drown it with water until every ember is wet, stir it and drown it again, then hold the back of your hand just above the ashes to feel for heat. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.

In normal times, New York allows campfires less than 3 feet high and 4 feet across, burning only charcoal or dry, clean, untreated wood, and they must never be left unattended. On New York state land in normal times, use only dead and down wood; cutting standing trees is prohibited.

Outdoors, asleep counts as unattended. If a fire must burn while people sleep, one person stays awake to watch it; otherwise put it out before you sleep (Army TC 21-3 gives this rule for snow caves in severe weather; this app applies it to any outdoor fire).
